summary: This experimental document specifies TCP-Friendly Multicast Congestion Control, a single-rate scheme for multicast in best-effort networks. The sender adapts to the receiver seeing the worst conditions. It competes reasonably fairly with TCP and keeps a smooth rate, which suits streaming media.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4654 defines TFMCC, a way to set the sending rate for a multicast stream. Each receiver works out the rate that would be fair for TCP on its own path, only a few of them report, and the sender slows down to the lowest rate anyone reported.

questions: how does multicast congestion control work
what is the current limiting receiver
subtitle: Multicast rate control where each receiver measures its own path and the sender follows the worst one.

tldr.problem: A multicast sender has one sending rate for a whole group, so it has to know which receiver is worst off, and it cannot ask every receiver for feedback without the replies swamping it.
tldr.mechanism: Every receiver measures the loss event rate and round-trip time on its own path and computes a rate that would be fair for TCP. A feedback suppression mechanism lets only some receivers report, and the sender follows the receiver that reported the lowest rate.
tldr.outcome: It is an Experimental document. The memo says TFMCC is reasonably fair with TCP and has a low variation of throughput, which suits streaming media, but is less responsive to a change in bandwidth than TCP is.

today: RFC 4654 is an Experimental document from August 2006, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The memo records that the Reliable Multicast Transport Working Group published it in the Experimental category while waiting for deployment and experience, with the intention of re-submitting it as a Proposed Standard once the scheme was judged adequate.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
TFMCC is a source-based, single-rate congestion control scheme that builds on the unicast TCP-Friendly Rate Control mechanism. It is stable and responsive under a wide range of network conditions and scales to receiver sets on the order of several thousand receivers. To support that scalability, as much congestion control functionality as possible is located at the receivers. Each receiver continuously determines a desired receive rate that is TCP-friendly for the path from the sender to itself, and selected receivers then report that rate to the sender in feedback packets.

TFMCC is a building block rather than a complete protocol. The memo specifies a congestion control mechanism that could be used in a transport protocol such as RTP, or in an application that does end-to-end congestion control at the application level. It does not discuss packet formats, reliability or implementation-related issues.

The memo defines the standard of fairness it aims for: a multicast flow is reasonably fair if its sending rate is generally within a factor of two of the sending rate of a TCP flow from the sender to the slowest receiver of the multicast group under the same network conditions. In general TFMCC has a low variation of throughput, which makes it suitable for applications where a relatively smooth sending rate matters, such as streaming media. The penalty for that smoothness is reduced responsiveness to changes in available bandwidth, so the memo says TFMCC should be used when the application needs smooth throughput, in particular avoiding halving of the sending rate in response to a single packet drop.

The memo also sets out the limits. TFMCC needs an estimate of the loss event rate, and that estimate may be inaccurate if only very few packets per round-trip time are received, so TFMCC should not be used together with TCP if the capacity of the bottleneck link is less than 30 kbit/s. TFMCC is designed for applications that use a fixed packet size and vary their sending rate in packets per second; applications such as packet audio that need a fixed interval between packets and vary packet size instead cannot use it.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender cannot give every viewer its own stream, so it has to pick one rate and the slowest path sets it. TFMCC keeps the rate steady, which suits video and audio, at the cost of reacting more slowly than TCP when the network changes.

sections.title: Protocol Overview and the Rate Equation
sections.content:
TFMCC extends the mechanisms of TFRC into the multicast domain. To compete fairly with TCP, each receiver individually measures the network conditions and calculates a rate that would be TCP-friendly on the path from the sender to itself. The rate comes from an equation for TCP throughput, which roughly describes TCP's sending rate as a function of the loss event rate, round-trip time and packet size. A loss event is defined as one or more lost or marked packets from the packets received during one round-trip time, where a marked packet carries a congestion indication from Explicit Congestion Notification.

The mechanism has five steps. Each receiver measures the loss event rate and its round-trip time to the sender. Each receiver uses that information, with the throughput equation, to derive a TCP-friendly sending rate. A distributed feedback suppression mechanism allows only a subset of receivers to give feedback, so that the sender is not swamped, and it is arranged so that a receiver reporting a low rate has a high probability of being allowed to speak. Receivers whose feedback is not suppressed report their calculated rate in receiver reports, which also let the receivers measure their round-trip time. The sender then selects the receiver that reports the lowest rate as the current limiting receiver: when feedback with an even lower rate arrives, that receiver becomes the limiting receiver and the sending rate drops to match it, and the rate rises when the limiting receiver reports a rate above the current sending rate.

The throughput equation the memo recommends is a slightly simplified version of the equation for Reno TCP. In it, X is the transmit rate in bits per second, s is the packet size in bytes, R is the round-trip time in seconds, and p is the loss event rate between 0.0 and 1.0, expressed as the number of loss events as a fraction of the number of packets transmitted. The memo notes that the equation used must reflect TCP's retransmit timeout behaviour, and that the assumptions implicit in the equation about the loss event rate have to be a reasonable match to how the loss rate is actually measured.

The memo does not specify packet formats, because TFMCC will be used with a transport protocol and the formats depend on it. It does give the header fields each side needs. A sender's packet carries a sequence number, a suppression rate, a send timestamp, a receiver ID with an echo of that receiver's last report timestamp, a flag saying whether that receiver is the current limiting receiver, a feedback round counter, and a maximum round-trip time value. A feedback packet carries a receiver ID, flags for whether the receiver has measured a round-trip time, has seen a loss event and is about to leave, a timestamp, an echo of the timestamp of the last data packet received, an echo of the feedback round counter, and the desired sending rate.
sections.plainLanguage: Each viewer computes what rate TCP would get on its own path, using a formula with three inputs: how often packets are lost, the round-trip time, and the packet size. The sender then follows the lowest of those numbers.

sections.title: The Sender Side
sections.content:
The sender multicasts data packets at a controlled rate, and whenever feedback arrives it checks whether it must switch the current limiting receiver and readjust the rate. Its main tasks are adjusting the sending rate, controlling receiver feedback and assisting the receivers' round-trip time measurements. At initialization the maximum round-trip time is set to a value larger than the highest round-trip time to any receiver, and it should not be smaller than 500 milliseconds for operation in the public Internet. The sending rate is initialized to one packet per maximum round-trip time.

The maximum round-trip time is computed from the feedback. For each feedback packet the sender computes the instantaneous round-trip time to that receiver. If it is larger than the current maximum, the maximum is raised to it. Otherwise, if no feedback with a higher instantaneous round-trip time arrives during a feedback round, the maximum is reduced to the larger of 0.9 times the current maximum and the peak receiver round-trip time measured during the round. The maximum is also never allowed to fall below the maximum interval between consecutive data packets, because feedback suppression is closely coupled to the sending of data packets.

Rate adjustment has four cases. If there is no limiting receiver, the reporting receiver becomes it and the rate is set to that receiver's rate, provided that would raise the rate by less than 8s divided by R_max bits per second, which is one packet per R_max; otherwise the rate is raised gradually at that rate every R_max seconds. If a receiver is not the limiting receiver and reports a lower rate, and has not set the leave flag, it becomes the limiting receiver and the rate drops to its value. If the limiting receiver has signalled that it is leaving, a new receiver becomes the limiting receiver, but the rate is not raised to that receiver's rate for the duration of a feedback round, so that other, slower receivers still get a chance to report. If the receiver is already the limiting receiver, the rate is set to the smaller of its rate and the current rate plus 8s divided by R_max bits per second.

Feedback is organised in rounds. A feedback round lasts six times the maximum round-trip time, or four times in the Any-Source Multicast case where feedback goes to the whole group. Only receivers that wish to report a rate below the current suppression rate, or whose round-trip time exceeds the maximum round-trip time, may send feedback. At the start of a round the suppression rate is set to the highest value that can be represented, and as feedback arrives it is lowered, so that more and more feedback is suppressed towards the end of the round. The parameter g sets how far a higher rate may suppress a lower one, and the memo recommends a value of 0.1, which guarantees that the lowest reported rate is within a factor of g of the true lowest rate among the receivers.

The sender also uses a slow start at the beginning of a session and after an idle period. During slow start the sending rate increases exponentially, limited to the minimum of the rates in the receiver reports, and receivers report twice the rate at which they currently receive data. Since a receiver can never receive data faster than its link bandwidth, this limits the overshoot to twice that bandwidth. Slow start ends as soon as any receiver experiences its first packet loss, because that receiver's calculated rate will then be below the current sending rate and it becomes the limiting receiver. If the sender stops sending for a while it records the current rate, and when it resumes it may slow start from the allowed rate back up to the recorded one.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender runs the show from the feedback it gets. It keeps the slowest report, lowers its rate to match it, and lets only the receivers that are genuinely struggling speak up, using a threshold that tightens as the round goes on.

sections.title: The Receiver Side
sections.content:
Receivers measure the network conditions, namely the round-trip time and the loss event rate, and use them to calculate a rate that is fair to competing traffic. The receiver is initialized when it receives the first data packet: the round-trip time is set to the maximum round-trip time carried in that packet and used until the first real measurement, the loss event rate is set to 0, and the flags for leaving, for having measured a round-trip time and for having seen a loss are cleared. A receiver that wishes to leave within the next feedback round sets the leave flag in its report, and if the leaving receiver is the current limiting receiver it should set the flag in all of its reports during that round.

The round-trip time is measured when a data packet arrives carrying the receiver's own ID. The sample is the time now minus the echoed report timestamp, and the smoothed estimate is updated as a weighted average of the previous estimate and the new sample. A filter parameter q of 0.5 is recommended for receivers that are not the current limiting receiver, and 0.9 for the limiting receiver, which measures far more often. The memo notes that TFMCC is not sensitive to the precise value of this constant.

The receiver also computes a one-way delay from the timestamp and the echoed report timestamp in the data packet, and uses it to correct the round-trip time estimate between measurements, so that a change in the forward path shows up before the next round-trip measurement. The clocks of the sender and the receivers need not be synchronized for this, because the clock skew cancels out when the two one-way measurements are added to form a round-trip estimate, as long as the drift between real measurements is negligible.

Before it has seen any loss event, a receiver cannot compute a TCP-friendly rate, so it measures the current receive rate over the last k round-trip times, with a value for k between 2 and 4 recommended, and reports twice that as its desired rate. Once it has measured a non-zero loss event rate, it computes the desired rate with the throughput equation, using the maximum round-trip time in place of its own round-trip time if no measurement is available yet. A receiver may decide not to report rates below one packet per 8 seconds, since a sender is slow to recover from such a rate, in which case it reports one packet per 8 seconds instead.

Feedback suppression at the receiver uses an exponentially weighted random timer. When a feedback round starts, a non-limiting receiver sets a timer to expire after a random fraction of the round, so that receivers spread their reports out. The current limiting receiver sends its feedback independently of all the others, once per round-trip time, and its feedback neither suppresses nor is suppressed by other feedback. The timer is cancelled if a data packet arrives carrying a lower suppression rate than the receiver's calculated rate, or with a higher or equal maximum round-trip time.
sections.plainLanguage: A receiver times the round trip and watches for missing packets, then turns those two numbers into a fair rate. Before it has seen any loss it has nothing to go on, so it reports twice what it is receiving. It waits a random slice of the round before reporting, so that thousands of receivers do not all speak at once.

sections.title: Calculating the Loss Event Rate
sections.content:
Obtaining an accurate and stable measurement of the loss event rate is of primary importance, and the measurement is performed at the receiver from the sequence numbers of the arriving packets. The loss of a packet is detected by the arrival of at least three packets with a higher sequence number, the same requirement as TCP, which makes TFMCC more robust in the presence of reordering. Unlike TCP, a packet that arrives late, after three later packets have arrived, can still fill the hole in the reception record and the receiver can recalculate the loss event rate. For an ECN-capable connection, a marked packet is detected as a congestion event as soon as it arrives, without waiting for later packets.

The receiver then maps the packet loss history into loss events, where a loss event is one or more packets lost in one round-trip time, so that the measurement is robust to several consecutive packets being lost as part of the same event. To decide whether a lost or marked packet starts a new event or belongs to an existing one, the receiver compares sequence numbers and timestamps. For a lost packet the nominal arrival time is interpolated from the arrival times of the last packet to arrive before it and the first to arrive after it, and the last packet of the previous event and the new loss are treated as part of the same event if the previous event's interpolated arrival time plus the round-trip time is not before the new one.

The loss event rate comes from the average loss interval, which is calculated with a filter that weights the most recent intervals so that the measured rate changes smoothly. The memo gives the weights and the example for n of 8, which are 1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 0.8, 0.6, 0.4 and 0.2. The value of n determines how fast TFMCC responds to changes in the level of congestion, and as specified it should not be used for values significantly greater than 8 for traffic that might compete with TCP in the global Internet. The loss event rate p is the reciprocal of the average loss interval.
sections.plainLanguage: A run of missing packets is counted as one event, not as many. The receiver then works out the average gap between events and takes the reciprocal, which is the loss event rate the rate formula needs. Recent events count for more than old ones, so the rate reacts but does not jump.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
TFMCC is not a transport protocol in its own right but a congestion control mechanism to be used with one, so security primarily has to be considered in the context of a specific transport protocol and its authentication mechanisms.

Congestion control mechanisms can potentially be exploited to create a denial of service, for example through spoofed feedback, so any transport protocol that uses TFMCC should ensure that feedback is accepted only from valid receivers of the data. The mechanisms can also potentially be manipulated by a greedy receiver that wants more than its fair share of bandwidth. In TFMCC a receiver can influence the sending rate only if it is the current limiting receiver, that is, if it has the lowest calculated rate of all receivers, and if that rate is manipulated to exceed the rate of the second lowest receiver it will stop being the limiting receiver. A greedy receiver can therefore only significantly increase the transmission rate if it is the only participant in the session. Against that case, possible defences normally include some form of nonce that the receiver must feed back to the sender to prove receipt, and the details would depend on the transport protocol and on whether it is reliable or unreliable.

The memo also notes that a receiver may send feedback claiming a very low calculated rate, which will reduce the rate of the multicast session and might render it useless, but cannot hurt the network itself. It expects protocols that incorporate ECN with TFMCC to use the ECN nonce, a modification to ECN that protects the sender from the accidental or malicious concealment of marked packets, and again leaves the details to the transport protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: The risk here is feedback that lies. A fake report could slow the whole session down, so the transport protocol has to check who feedback comes from. A greedy receiver cannot gain much, because it only influences the rate while it is the slowest receiver.

items.title: Three packets to confirm a loss
items.text: A packet counts as lost once three packets with higher sequence numbers have arrived.

items.title: Marked packets
items.text: On an ECN-capable connection a marked packet is a congestion event as soon as it arrives.

items.title: Interpolated arrival time
items.text: The nominal arrival time of a lost packet is interpolated from the packets before and after it.

items.title: One event per round trip
items.text: Several packets lost within one round-trip time count as a single loss event.

items.title: Weighted intervals
items.text: The average loss interval weights the recent intervals more heavily, so the rate changes smoothly.
